uncited: Unlike its sibling [Phong Shading](1853-phong-shading.md), which interpolates normals across a polygon, this method computes lighting per-voxel or per-pixel using the local geometry at the hit point.

*   **Inputs**: Surface normal $\mathbf{N}$ at the hit point; light direction vector $\mathbf{L}$ (from surface to light); view direction vector $\mathbf{V}$ (from surface to camera); light color/intensity $I_{light}$; ambient light color/intensity $I_{ambient}$; object diffuse color coefficient $k_d$; object specular color coefficient $k_s$; specular power/shininess $k$ (or $n$).
The method operates on scalar color values and 3D vectors.
No complex data structures are required beyond the standard ray-tracing intersection data (position, normal).
This represents light emanating from a direct source bouncing off the surface.
The calculation involves a constant number of vector operations (dot products, normalization, exponentiation).
No precomputed tables or large buffers are required.
*   **Limitations**: The Blinn-Phong specular term is an approximation and does not strictly conserve energy or follow physical BRDFs as accurately as microfacet models.
*   **When to use**: Real-time rendering, volume visualization where performance is critical, or when a simple "shiny" look is desired without the cost of more complex models.
*   **When not to use**: Physically based rendering (PBR) requiring strict energy conservation, or when accurate specular distribution is critical for scientific accuracy.
It became a standard in computer graphics for shading surfaces.
